rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators place the surah early in Mecca, eighth in chronological order after surah 81.
rows.anchor: the majority maintain that it is early Makkan. It is often placed eighth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some place the first portion in Mecca and the last in Medina because verses 14–15 mention prayer and alms associated with Eid al-Fitr, established only in Medina.
rows.anchor: Some consider the first part of the sūrah to be Makkan and the last part to be Madinan

rows.speaker: family of the Prophet
rows.claim: Family narrations interpret the prayer and alms in verses 14–15 as those of Eid al-Fitr.
rows.anchor: according to narrations from the family of the Prophet, refer to “the prayer and zakāh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others hold that the whole surah is Meccan despite anticipating the later Eid rites.
rows.anchor: Others say that it can still refer to these ritual practices, although it was revealed before them

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly recommended surahs 87 and 88 for evening prayer and often recited them at both Eids and Friday prayer.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is said to have recommended reciting Sūrahs 87 and 88 for the evening prayer

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly advised reciting this surah during prostration.
rows.anchor: He is also said to have advised his followers to recite it while in prostration

rows.speaker: Imam ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: Ali said that knowing its blessing would prompt ten daily recitations; reciting it amounts to reciting the Quran and scriptures of Moses and Abraham.
rows.anchor: according to Imam ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, if people knew what a blessing al-Aʿlā has

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah moves from glorification and encouragement to reception or rejection of the reminder, worldly preference, and continuity with earlier revelation.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with glorification of God (vv. 1–5) and encouragement for the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises to give revelation at the proper time and preserve it in the Prophet's memory.
rows.anchor: This verse is an assurance that God will grant revelation in due time and ensure the Prophet does not forget it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel's arrival prompted the Prophet to recite the passage's beginning before Gabriel finished, fearing forgetfulness; this occasion occasioned the verse.
rows.anchor: the Prophet would sometimes recite the beginning of the passage being revealed before Gabriel had finished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 20:114 and 75:16–17 likewise counsel the Prophet against hastening revelation.
rows.anchor: In 20:114 and 75:16–17, the Prophet is also counseled not to “hasten” the revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators assign an early Meccan origin, probably soon after surah 101; others place it early in Medina.
rows.anchor: Most commentators maintain that al-ʿĀdiyāt was revealed in the early Makkan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meccan attribution rests on style; Medinan attribution rests on some interpretations of its subject matter.
rows.anchor: The case for Makkan attribution is supported by its similarity in style to other Makkan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One revelation account concerns Mundhir ibn Amr's expedition to Banu Kinanah; after delayed news, hypocrites claimed all were killed, and revelation reported the expedition's horses.
rows.anchor: the hypocrites said, “They have all been killed,” and so God gave news about this expedition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some connect the oaths with Badr, although a report from Ali says only two horses were there, the remaining mounts being camels.
rows.anchor: according to an account attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib there were only two horses at Badr

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: Another Ali report identifies the oaths with pilgrims rushing on mounts from Arafat through Muzdalifah to Mina.
rows.anchor: Another account attributed to ʿAlī sees these oaths as depictions of that portion of the ḥajj pilgrimage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Five charger oaths precede human ingratitude and love of possessions; the ending warns of judgment of inward states.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with five oaths by various forms of charging horses

rows.speaker: al-Bayḍāwī
rows.claim: The oaths can allegorize charging souls who transmit holy light, kindle knowledge, attack whims, desire God, and enter Illiyyun.
rows.anchor: According to al-Bayḍāwī, the oaths in these verses can also be seen as an allusion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Occasion reports support either battle horses or pilgrimage camels, and the oath can encompass both as worthy functions.
rows.anchor: it can be seen as applying to both, as each is understood as fulfilling a function

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hooves striking rocks produce the sparks.
rows.anchor: The striking of hooves on rocks causes sparks to fly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pilgrimage camels hurry from Mashar to Mina at dawn on the Day of Sacrifice.
rows.anchor: The camels that rush from Mashʿar to Minā do so at dawn on the Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final oath depicts horses penetrating enemy ranks or camels rushing from Mashar to Mina.
rows.anchor: the horses penetrated to the center of the enemy troops (Bḍ) or to the rush of camels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will teach Muhammad the Quran and guard him from forgetting it except what God wills.
rows.anchor: سنقرئك يا محمد هذا القرآن فلا تنساه ،   إلاّ ما شاء الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some read this as divine teaching and preservation and an instruction against hurried recitation, as in 75:16–17.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم :  هذا إخبار من الله نبيه عليه الصلاة والسلام أنه يعلمه هذا القرآن

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The Prophet mentally rehearsed the Quran for fear of forgetting it.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد ،   قوله :  سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلا تَنْسَى قال :  كان يتذكر القرآن في نفسه مخافة أن ينسى

rows.speaker: قائلو هذه المقالة
rows.claim: The exception denotes material God wills him to forget, namely abrogated text whose ruling and recitation God removes.
rows.anchor: فقال قائلو هذه المقالة :  معنى الاستثناء في هذا الموضع على النسيان

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The Prophet forgot nothing except what God willed.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلا تَنْسَى كان صلى الله عليه وسلم لا ينسى شيئا إلاّ ما شاءَ اللّهُ

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others interpret forgetting as abandoning practice: the Prophet must act on all revelation except rulings God abrogates.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون :  معنى النسيان في هذا الموضع :  الترك

rows.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
rows.claim: An Arabic language authority says the exception preserves divine discretion without implying God actually wills any forgetting, like 11:107–108 and conventional oath exceptions.
rows.anchor: وكان بعض أهل العربية يقول في ذلك :  لم يشأ الله أن تنسى شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabari prefers actual exception for what God causes the Prophet to forget by abrogating and removing it; this is the most apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: والقول الذي هو أولى بالصواب عندي ،   قول من قال :  معنى ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The runners are horses; another Ibn Abbas report specifies warfare, and he says only horses and dogs pant this way.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس ،   في قوله {  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  الخيل

rows.speaker: عكرِمة
rows.claim: The referents are horses, whose panting can be heard when they run.
rows.anchor: عن عكرِمة في قوله :  {  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  الخيل

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Only dogs and horses among animals pant in this manner; he also identifies the runners as horses.
rows.anchor: عن عطاء ،   قال :  ليس شيء من الدوابّ يضبح غير الكلب والفرس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The verse depicts panting horses.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد ،   في قوله الله :  {  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  الخيل تَضْبَح

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Horses run until they pant.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة ،   قوله :  {  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  هي الخيل ،   عَدَتْ حَتى ضَبَحَتْ

rows.speaker: سالم
rows.claim: He reads the runners as horses running so hard they pant.
rows.anchor: سمعت سالما يقرأ :  {  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  هي الخيل عدت ضبحا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: The runners are horses.
rows.anchor: سمعت الضحاك يقول في قوله :  {  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  هي الخيل

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Ibn Masud identifies the runners as camels; one report describes their panting as breathing.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله{  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  هي الإبل إذا ضبحت تنفّست

rows.speaker: إبراهيم
rows.claim: The runners are camels.
rows.anchor: عن إبراهيم {  وَالْعَادِياتِ ضَبْحا } قال :  الإبل

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: The runners are camels.
rows.anchor: عن عبيد بن عمير ،   قال :  هي الإبل ،   يعني {  وَالْعادِياتِ ضَبْحا }

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The scene belongs to the pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: قال :  قال ابن مسعود :  هو في الحجّ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In an account later retracted, Ibn Abbas takes the horses as raiding for God, then returning at night to cook and kindle fire.
rows.anchor: فقلت له :  الخيل حين تغير في سبيل الله ،   ثم تأوي إلى الليل

rows.speaker: عليّ بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali rebukes Ibn Abbas's horse interpretation: only Zubayr and Miqdad had horses at Badr, so the runners are pilgrim mounts from Arafat via Muzdalifah to Mina.
rows.anchor: والله لكانت أوّل غزوة في الإسلام لِبدر ،   وما كان معنا إلا فرسان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: After Ali's correction Ibn Abbas withdrew his horse interpretation and adopted Ali's.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس :  فنزعت عن قولي ،   ورجعت إلى الذي قال عليّ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabari prefers horses, since camels do not pant in the stated manner, whereas horses do.
rows.anchor: وأولى القولين في ذلك عندي بالصواب :  قول من قال :  عني بالعاديات :  الخيل

rows.speaker: عليّ
rows.claim: Ali distinguishes a horse's pant as a humming sound from a camel's breath.
rows.anchor: قال عليّ رضي الله عنه :  الضبح من الخيل :  الحَمْحَمة ،   ومن الإبل :  النفس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas imitates the sound of panting as ah ah.
rows.anchor: سمعت ابن عباس يصف الضبح :  أَحْ أَحْ
